title: Assessment of Mark‐Recapture Efforts in 2020–2025 Provides Updated Insights on Population Dynamics for Female Loggerheads (Caretta caretta) Nesting at Dalyan Beach, Türkiye
content:
ABSTRACT

Accurately estimating the demographics and abundance of sea turtles is critical for their conservation. Sea turtles are highly migratory posing a challenge to accurately monitor the in-water populations. Fortunately, monitoring nesting beaches allows us to estimate the abundance of the most important demographic group: breeding age females. This study aimed to evaluate the mark-recapture efforts across the 2020–2025 nesting seasons to assess double tagging and characterize the population dynamics of female loggerhead turtles (Caretta caretta) at Dalyan Beach, Türkiye, a critical nesting beach in the Mediterranean Sea. We collected re-encounter rates across seasons, examined tag loss, nesting trends, nesting frequency and carapace size. A low proportion of females (n = 47 of 665 tagged) was observed with lost tags, with no significant difference between tag placements (p > 0.05). We observed a greater proportion of newly tagged females (65.3%–76.6%) relative to recaptured individuals with most females (91%) nesting at least once across the seasons. We estimated an internesting interval of 12 days, an estimated clutch frequency of 1.8 and a remigration interval of 2.4 years. The mean curved carapace length was 75.18 cm (±4.76). The increasing number of females nesting for the first time and increasing abundance of a mean of 684 (±128.6) nests per season compared to historical data suggest the potential positive outcomes of conservation efforts implemented in the earlier decades. Our observed high tag retention rate has highlighted the effectiveness of this simple, low-cost methodology for estimating the population dynamics of sea turtles.
